parsed_answer.content:
In the Java Virtual Machine, execution contexts are categorized strictly into user threads and daemon threads. Understanding the operational distinction between daemon threads and user threads is critical for writing robust concurrent applications that terminate cleanly without hanging or leaving orphan processes in the background. A user thread is a standard execution thread created by application code or the main entry point of a program. The JVM runtime maintains a vital invariant: it will continue running as long as at least one active user thread is alive, regardless of whether the main method has returned.

Conversely, a daemon thread is a background service thread—such as the Garbage Collector (GC), reference processors, or background monitoring tasks—whose execution life cycle is entirely subordinate to the application. Daemon threads do not prevent the JVM from exiting. The exact moment the final user thread finishes its execution stack and terminates, the JVM initiates a hard shutdown sequence, abruptly terminating all active daemon threads without executing their finally blocks, catching InterruptedException, or flushing I/O buffers. You designate a thread as a daemon thread by invoking `Thread.setDaemon(true)` prior to starting the thread. If you attempt to mutate this flag after the thread has already started, the JVM throws an `IllegalThreadStateException`.

items: Thread Inheritance Rule: When a new thread is spawned from an existing active thread, the child thread automatically inherits the daemon status of its parent. A daemon thread always spawns child daemon threads, while a user thread spawns user threads by default.

JVM Termination Sequence: When the active user thread count drops to zero, the JVM stops all application threads concurrently. It does not wait for daemon threads to finish looping or processing current instructions, which can lead to data corruption if daemon threads perform mid-flight database writes.

The java.lang.Thread API: The boolean flag `daemon` is stored internally within the native thread state structures. Modifying it is strictly prohibited post-initialization because underlying OS-level thread attributes are already bound during `pthread_create` or equivalent native calls.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production anti-pattern is writing critical resource-release routines, file-closing handlers, or persistent transaction rollbacks inside daemon threads. Because the JVM exits the exact instant the final user thread stops, daemon threads do not respect finally blocks or try-with-resources cleanups during shutdown. If you rely on a daemon thread to flush an audit log or close a connection pool, you will experience silent data truncation and mysterious resource leaks. Always use explicit shutdown hooks (Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook) for tasks that must execute during application teardown.
